source.title: LightDefense: A Lightweight Uncertainty-Driven Defense against Jailbreaks via Shifted Token Distribution
source.authors: Zhuo-Ran Yang; Jie Peng; Zhen Tan; Tian-Long Chen; Yan-Yong Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates adversarial suffix attacks on safety-trained chat models and reports harmful-compliance rates. It does not test fine-tuning, but this is a different-method test of the suffix-attack part of V4.
record.gate_note: The paper reports ASR for GCG and AmpleGCG attacks, which it describes as using adversarial suffixes. It also qualitatively examines distributions of the first few response tokens for safe and unsafe answers, but does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL. It does not test fine-tuning, compliant prefills, decoding changes as bypasses, weight localization, the cause of shallowness, or training to deepen safety.
record.test_reason: This is a defense paper. It builds on the observation that the first tokens set a response's direction, adjusts token probabilities over only the first m=3 decoding steps, and reports its own method's ASR against baselines. The no-defense ASRs are standard attack baselines run to evaluate the defense. The paper does not test whether shallow alignment holds: there is no KL analysis, no fine-tuning, no prefilling, and no check that suffix attacks work by getting past the opening tokens.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude that LightDefense, a training-free, uncertainty-adaptive shift of token distributions over the first decoding steps, sharply reduces jailbreak ASR on Qwen3-8b and Llama3.1-8b while largely preserving helpfulness and adding negligible overhead.
record.recipe_differences: This is an inference-time token-distribution defense, not fine-tuning or aligned-versus-base KL analysis. It adjusts distributions for the first m tokens and evaluates jailbreak attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by target model and attack method. The paper also reports hyperparameter sensitivity, noting that τ affects the safety-helpfulness balance.

fits_no_version.finding: On Qwen3, safe and unsafe responses separate in a 2D PCA of first-token probability distributions; no number is given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: First-token output distributions distinguish safe from unsafe responses under jailbreak.

fits_no_version.finding: Shifting token probabilities toward refusal tokens over only the first 3 decoding steps cuts keyword-based ASR to near 0% for most attacks. Appendix C reports rare cases where the model refuses at first and then complies later.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering only the opening tokens at inference largely blocks jailbreaks, though late compliance after an initial refusal can still occur.

record.problems: Only two models are evaluated. Results are based on 3 algorithm runs, but no error bars or other uncertainty estimates are stated. The first-token analysis is qualitative and does not report the aligned-versus-base KL measure in V3.

untested.parts: No prefilling or decoding-change attacks. Suffix-attack ASRs appear only as defense baselines, and their mechanism is not examined.
The cause of shallowness is not examined.
No training-based deepening. LightDefense is an inference-time adjustment of the first tokens only.

missing.what: No-defense ASRs for AutoDAN, PAIR and CipherChat on both models. CipherChat is 83% on Qwen3 and 30% on Llama3.1; the other columns are ambiguous because the headers are garbled.
Qualitative case where the model refuses initially but later complies under GCG even with LightDefense applied.
missing.versions: V7-adjacent; this is the paper's own method

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T2/tests classification is downgraded to T4: the paper uses the first-token observation (citing GCG, Zou et al.) as a design tool and evaluates a defense. Table 2 column order cannot be read reliably from the extracted text, so the reader's attack-specific baseline ASRs may be misassigned. ASR is keyword-based. Results are averaged over 3 runs with no error bars. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning and refusal after fine-tuning.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Aligned-versus-base per-token KL across response positions.
Compliant-opening prefills and decoding changes as bypasses; the study tests GCG and AmpleGCG suffix attacks but does not establish that getting past initial tokens is their mechanism.
Whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Training safety to extend beyond initial tokens and testing its durability.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Qwen3-8b with no defense, GCG and AmpleGCG suffix attacks
reader_labels.reason: Both attacks have ASR of 88% without defense, showing substantial harmful compliance in these tested conditions (r1, r3).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Llama3.1-8b with no defense, GCG and AmpleGCG suffix attacks
reader_labels.reason: Attack success is much lower than on Qwen3-8b: 18% for GCG and 2% for AmpleGCG (r5, r7).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: GCG and AmpleGCG suffix attacks with LightDefense on both models
reader_labels.reason: The reported ASR is 0% for both suffix attacks on both tested models when LightDefense is applied (r2, r4, r6, r8).
